step_1_color.question: What is the bird's PRIMARY COLOR from aerial view?
step_1_color.help_text: Look at the dominant body color. This is visible even from high altitude.

options.label: WHITE/PALE
options.description: Pure white or very pale gray plumage (Pelicans, Egrets, Terns)

options.label: DARK/BLACK
options.description: Black, very dark brown, or dark gray (Cormorants, Anhingas, Skimmers, Noddies)

options.label: BLUE-GRAY
options.description: Blue-gray, slate, or ash colored (Herons, Night-Herons)

options.label: BROWN/REDDISH
options.description: Brown, reddish-brown, or mixed dark colors (Reddish Egret, Ibis)

options.label: PINK/RED
options.description: Bright pink or reddish overall (Spoonbill - unmistakable!)

WHITE.question: What is the BILL SHAPE and LENGTH?
WHITE.help_text: Look at the bill carefully - shape is diagnostic even from aerial view.

options.label: LONG STRAIGHT
options.description: Long, straight, needle-like bill (Egrets, Herons, Stork)

DARK.question: What is the BILL SHAPE and LENGTH?
DARK.help_text: Bill shape helps separate cormorants from pelicans and skimmers.

options.label: HOOKED
options.description: Medium length with hooked tip (Cormorants, Anhingas)

options.label: HUGE RED
options.description: Massive red bill with longer lower mandible (Black Skimmer)

BLUE.question: What is the BILL SHAPE and LENGTH?
BLUE.help_text: Bill length helps separate large herons from smaller ones.

options.label: VERY LONG
options.description: Very long, straight bill (Great Blue Heron)

BROWN.question: What is the BILL SHAPE and LENGTH?
BROWN.help_text: Curved bills indicate ibis/spoonbill. Straight bills indicate herons or shorebirds.

PINK.question: CONFIRMATION - Roseate Spoonbill?

options.label: YES - BRIGHT PINK

notes.changes: Replaced size-based Step 1 with COLOR (more reliable for aerial view). Added BILL SHAPE as Step 2 (highly diagnostic for aerial imagery).
notes.source: Based on Cornell Lab of Ornithology, Audubon Society, and Gulf Coast avian monitoring protocols
accuracy_tips: COLOR is most reliable from aerial view - always start here
BILL SHAPE is diagnostic even at distance - curved vs straight is obvious
Use colony context - species often segregate by habitat
Use relative comparison - if multiple birds visible, compare sizes
Use historical data - colonies often have same dominant species year to year
Use location - some species are restricted to specific regions
When uncertain, use combination codes (WHEG, CARO, UNIB, etc.)
common_mistakes: Confusing size from different camera heights - use COLOR first instead
GREG vs SNEG - GREG is noticeably larger, but also look at bill color (yellow vs black)
ROYT vs SATE - bill color (orange vs black with yellow tip) is diagnostic
DCCO vs NECO - size and range, often cannot distinguish from aerial view (use UNCO)
LTBH vs TRHE - TRHE has white belly stripe visible when perched
Tern species - often impossible without bill color/size details (use UNTE if uncertain)
